teach: From the lesson: Spanish says you have hunger, the way you have a coat or a key.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Tengo hambre — I am hungry. Word for word, I have hunger. Tengo means I have. Hambre means hunger.' Another way to hold it: tengo is I have, and hambre is the hunger you are carrying.
walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson starts in your body, before the restaurant. (2) Tengo means I have, and hambre means hunger. (3) I have hunger is how Spanish says: I am hungry.

teach: From the lesson: thirst is built the exact same way as hunger.
teach2: From the lesson: 'Tengo sed — I am thirsty. I have thirst. Sed means thirst. Tengo sed. Notice sed is a short word, one clean beat: sed.' From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Tengo sed — I am thirsty. I have thirst. Sed means thirst. Tengo sed.' Another way: hambre and sed are brothers — tengo carries both, hunger and thirst.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Tengo hambre means I am hungry, built on tengo, I have. (2) Sed is the word Carmen defines as thirst. (3) So tengo sed means: I am thirsty.

teach: From the lesson: quiero is the verb that runs every restaurant on earth.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Quiero — I want. Quiero. It comes from querer — to want, and also to love' Another way: quiero is the handle — attach any dish or drink to it and you have an order.
walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson gives one strong handle for ordering. (2) That handle is quiero, from querer. (3) Quiero means: I want.

teach: From the lesson: the first thing on the table, in any country where the sun is hot.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'El agua — the water. Agua means water. And I know, your eye just caught something' Another way: agua lives inside words like aquarium — the water is right there in it.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Carmen puts the first drink on the table before anything else. (2) Agua is the word she defines as water. (3) El agua means: the water.

teach: From the lesson: the detail that separates ordering like you live there from pointing at a picture.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Sin hielo — without ice. Sin means without. Hielo means ice. And there is our silent h again' Another way: sin is without, hielo is ice — hielo sounds like YEH-loh, its h silent.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Sin means without — the lesson defines it directly. (2) Hielo means ice. (3) Together, sin hielo means: without ice.

teach: From the lesson: the first meal of the day, the fast-breaker.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'El desayuno — breakfast. Desayuno means breakfast. It is a longer word, so let us walk it in pieces' Another way: desayuno and breakfast tell the same story — both mean breaking the night's fast.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Carmen pauses the drinks to put the first meal of the day on the table. (2) That meal is el desayuno. (3) El desayuno is: breakfast.

q: Bill wants the famous plate, rice with chicken, and wants to order it politely. What should he say?
answer: Quiero arroz con pollo, por favor
accept: I want rice with chicken, please
choices: Quiero arroz con pollo, por favor
Quiero agua sin hielo, por favor
mcAnswer: Quiero arroz con pollo, por favor
teach: From the lesson: quiero, the thing, por favor — the whole machine in one breath.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Quiero arroz con pollo, por favor — I want rice with chicken, please. Say it with me, slowly first' Another way: arroz con pollo is rice with chicken, quiero asks for it, and por favor keeps it gentlemanly.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Quiero means I want, and por favor is the polite ending. (2) The famous plate is arroz con pollo, rice with chicken. (3) Joined in the lesson's order, the order is: Quiero arroz con pollo, por favor.

q: The first bite is wonderful, and Bill wants to pay the cook the compliment Carmen taught him. What does 'Está delicioso' mean?
teach: From the lesson: the sentence that turns a customer into a guest.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Está delicioso — it is delicious. Está means it is — the is for how something is right now, its condition in this moment. Delicioso means delicious.' Another way: está describes how the food is right now, and delicioso is the cook's favorite word to hear.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Está means it is, for how something is in this moment. (2) Delicioso means delicious. (3) Está delicioso means: it is delicious.

q: Bill is ordering drinks for the table. Jillian takes her water without ice. What line orders her water the way she takes it?
answer: Para ella, agua sin hielo, por favor
accept: for her, water without ice, please
choices: Para ella, agua sin hielo, por favor
mcAnswer: Para ella, agua sin hielo, por favor
teach: From the lesson: para ella is the signpost that tells the waiter where her glass belongs.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Para ella, agua sin hielo, por favor — for her, water without ice, please. Because you know how she takes it, Bill.' Another way: para ella means for her, agua is water, and sin hielo handles the ice.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Para ella means for her — the order is for Jillian. (2) Agua is water, and she takes it sin hielo, without ice. (3) The full line is: Para ella, agua sin hielo, por favor.

q: The meal is finished and Bill is ready to settle up like a gentleman. What does he say?
teach: From the lesson: the last scene of every good meal has its own line.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'La cuenta, por favor — the check, please. Cuenta means the check, the bill, the account of the meal.' Another way: cuenta is family to count and account — la cuenta is the counting of the meal.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Tengo hambre opens a meal; it cannot close one. (2) Cuenta means the check, the account of the meal. (3) With por favor keeping it polite, the closing line is: La cuenta, por favor.

q: In your own words: what does 'tengo' literally mean, and how does Carmen use it to build both the hunger sentence and the thirst sentence?
teach: From the lesson: tengo is the frame, and hambre and sed are what it carries.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Tengo plus a thing you feel in your body equals how you say you feel it. Tengo hambre, tengo sed.'
walk: Walk it through: (1) Tengo means I have. (2) Hambre is hunger and sed is thirst. (3) So Spanish reports both feelings the same way: I have hunger, I have thirst.
